official_version: "The Kestrel shaft was capped because the exchanger fire had made the lower workings unsafe. The drill core was left on its cradle because no lift could be slotted before the calving window closed."
actual_version: "The workings had been stable for eighty days when the cap went on, and there were two clear windows in that time. The core was left because raising it would have obliged the co-op to have it assessed, and an installation with an assessed asset in it can be sold by a vote of its own members. The cap was a board decision about ownership, written up as a safety measure."
who_knows_what:

Hour zero of this book is the hour the cap went on, which is a convenience of the co-op's
reckoning and not an accident: everything anyone at Kestrel argues about is dated from it.

The official account is on the board and has never been challenged, because every clause of
it is separately true. The workings had burned. A lift had been missed. The core is heavy and
the window is fifty-two hours. What the account does not contain is the eighty days between
the survey and the cap, in which nothing was unsafe and nothing was lifted.

Vance has read the notice perhaps a hundred times and holds the official version, not because
she believes the board but because she has never had a reason to count the days. Quiej wrote
the schedule that left the two windows empty. Between those two positions is most of the
pressure in the first half of the book, and neither of them has ever said any of it out loud.
